chunks: Characterizing CPU performance. The question: How do you characterize CPU performance?
The most honest measure of CPU performance is how long it takes to finish real work.
That time splits into three factors: the number of instructions, the average clock cycles each needs (CPI), and the length of one clock cycle.
Clock frequency alone tells you very little, because two chips at the same GHz can differ a lot in CPI.
Picture comparing two restaurants. You could ask how fast the chef chops, but that is only one piece.
What you care about is how long one diner waits (latency) and how many dinners go out per hour (throughput).
The fair test is a real busy evening of orders, not a single fast demo. Benchmarks do the same for CPUs, running a standard set of real programs.
Each extra 1% of memory accesses that go to DRAM adds 0. 45 to CPI. Beyond about 0. 85% the DRAM term is bigger than the branch and L2 stalls combined (0. 384).
This is why memory behavior, not core width, is often the first thing to examine.
Instruction count: how many instructions the program needs. CPI: average clock cycles per instruction. Its inverse is IPC, instructions per cycle.
Clock period: the time of one cycle, 1 divided by the frequency. Latency vs throughput: how long one task takes, versus how many tasks finish per second.
Benchmark: a standard set of programs run to compare machines.
Run a program of 10 to the 9 instructions on two chips. Chip A runs at 3 gigahertz with CPI 2, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 2 over (3 times 10 to the 9) about 0. 67 seconds.
Chip B runs at only 2 gigahertz with CPI 1, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1 over (2 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 50 seconds. The slower clock wins.
In the page's own example, halving a cache miss rate cuts CPI from 2. 5 to 1. 75, which is more than a 40% faster clock would give.
That is the whole idea: judge by time on real work.
"Performance is execution time. The Iron Law says time is instruction count times CPI times clock period, so clock speed alone is meaningless.
I'd measure with representative benchmarks like SPEC, summarize with a geometric mean, and separate latency from throughput.
Then look at what limits it: memory stalls, branch mispredicts, Amdahl's law, and finally performance per watt and thermal throttling."
